name: CDN or bot-management engineer
oneLine: Verifies signatures at the edge and separates good agents from bad bots.
goals: Verify RFC 9421 signatures at the edge in a few milliseconds and pass a trusted-agent verdict to the origin.
Fetch and cache keys from multiple directories (Visa, Mastercard, Web Bot Auth, UCP JWK sets) with sane rotation.
Enforce time windows and nonce uniqueness at scale across many points of presence.
Keep scrapers and credential-stuffing bots out while letting verified shopping agents through.
Give merchants a simple policy knob: block, allow verified, allow all, with per-path rules.
Report agent traffic separately from human and bot traffic.
pains: TAP, Web Bot Auth, UCP and Mastercard use the same signature mechanism with different tags, keyid formats and directory locations.
The minimum covered components in TAP omit @method, @query and a content digest, so a verified request can still be tampered with.
Nonce tracking is optional in some specs, and global nonce state across edges is expensive.
Key directories are controlled by single vendors, and an outage or key rotation breaks verification for everyone.
A verified agent is not a safe agent. Signatures prove who sent a request, not whether it will abuse the catalog or checkout.
Sample code in vendor repositories deviates from RFC 9421, and merchants copy it.
decisions: Which directories to trust and how to handle unknown keyids.
Whether to require a content digest and more covered components than the spec minimum.
Nonce storage strategy and replay window.
How to label and route agent traffic (Direct versus Intermediary, browse versus pay).
